title: Arvada
name: Arvada
metaDescription: Arvada 1031 exchange coordination spanning Olde Town's transit-oriented retail and the newer Standley Lake side, with guidance matched to each submarket's asset mix.

sections.html: Arvada runs on Olde Town and the G Line now. The historic core drives retail, the new commuter rail station drives everything getting built near it, and a 1031 buyer needs to know which of those two forces is behind the property in front of them before assuming either one applies. The city stretches across parts of Jefferson and Adams counties too, which shows up in permitting more than most buyers expect.

sections.heading: Two Different Arvadas
sections.html: Old Arvada, centered on Olde Town's brick storefronts, trades on charm and walkability. West Arvada, out toward Standley Lake, trades on newer residential rooftops and the retail built to serve them. A seller's replacement strategy should match which Arvada they're actually selling out of, because the tenant profile and lease terms differ more than the short drive between them suggests. A buyer who treats these two halves of the same city as one uniform market usually ends up underwriting the wrong risks. Rent per square foot on Olde Town's historic storefronts often runs higher than a comparable west-side box, even when the west-side building is newer and larger, since walkable character commands its own premium in this city.

sections.heading: What's Moving in Exchanges
sections.html:
Small mixed-use and retail buildings near Olde Town's rail station have picked up since the G Line opened, drawing transit-oriented redevelopment interest. Newer grocery-anchored centers near Standley Lake serve the west-side rooftops. Light industrial and flex space is limited but present along the Ralston Road corridor. Multifamily along the rail corridor has also drawn out-of-state capital in recent years, which has pushed pricing on well-located parcels above what a purely local buyer pool would have supported on its own. The categories that show up most:

  • Mixed-use and retail buildings near the Olde Town G Line station
  • Grocery-anchored retail serving the Standley Lake rooftop base
  • Small light industrial and flex space along Ralston Road
  • Multifamily near the commuter rail corridor
  • DST interests for owners consolidating out of direct management

sections.heading: The 45-Day Clock Doesn't Care Which Arvada You're In
sections.html: Whether the relinquished property sits in Olde Town or out by Standley Lake, the 45-day identification window runs the same. What changes is where the seller should be looking. An Olde Town seller needs to watch transit-oriented listings closely, since that inventory turns over fast and doesn't sit long. A west-side seller has more retail comparables to choose from and less urgency, but shouldn't mistake that for permission to delay the search entirely.

sections.heading: Diligence Specific to Transit-Adjacent Property
sections.html: Anything near the G Line station carries redevelopment interest, which can mean zoning overlays and design review requirements a buyer needs to understand before assuming as-of-right improvements. Older Olde Town buildings also carry more deferred maintenance risk than the newer west-side retail stock. A property condition assessment matters more on the historic side of town, and a buyer should ask specifically what work, if any, was done to bring an older building up to current code before the current ownership took over.

sections.heading: Coordinating With the Right Advisors
sections.html: The qualified intermediary needs the relinquished sale details early, and the investor's CPA should weigh in on which Arvada asset class fits the investor's broader portfolio before the identification list gets finalized. I've seen sellers pick a transit-oriented property because it looked exciting, then discover mid-exchange it didn't match what their CPA had modeled for depreciation and hold period. That conversation is far cheaper to have before an offer goes in than after. I also confirm early which county holds jurisdiction over a given Arvada parcel, since Jefferson and Adams counties don't always process permits on the same timeline, and a permit delay in one jurisdiction has thrown off more than one closing schedule here.

faqs.q: Is Olde Town Arvada property near the G Line station a good 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: It can be, but confirm the zoning overlay and any design review requirements before assuming you can make changes after closing. Transit-oriented listings also move fast, so build your identification list before the relinquished sale closes rather than during the 45-day window, when time is already tight.

faqs.q: Should I compare Olde Town and west Arvada the same way?
faqs.a: No. Olde Town trades on walkability and historic character, while the Standley Lake side trades on newer rooftops and grocery-anchored retail. The tenant profile and lease terms differ enough that the same underwriting approach won't fit both halves of the city.

faqs.q: Is light industrial space along Ralston Road available for exchange?
faqs.a: Some exists, but supply is limited compared to the retail and mixed-use inventory elsewhere in Arvada. A buyer set on industrial product may need to widen the search to neighboring submarkets rather than waiting on Ralston Road inventory alone, since new listings there come up infrequently and rarely stay on the market long once they do.

faqs.q: How does my CPA factor into choosing between Olde Town and west-side Arvada property?
faqs.a: Depreciation schedules and expected hold periods can differ meaningfully between an older mixed-use building and a newer retail center, so involve your CPA before finalizing the identification list, not after you've already fallen for a property that doesn't fit the plan.

faqs.q: Does 1031 Exchange Denver recommend specific Arvada properties to buy?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates identification logistics and communication among the investor's advisors and property contacts. Which property to pursue is the investor's decision, made with input from their CPA and qualified intermediary.
